explanation:
## What the grid is made of

Every input is a background of 0 with a few colour-8 objects. Each object is a closed outline that encloses one or more empty pockets (holes): some are single rings (one hole), some are two rings fused side by side or stacked (two holes), and some are longer chains of three or four rings. The outputs keep every cell exactly where it is; only the colour of each object changes, and different objects in the same grid get different colours (1, 2, 3, 4).

So this is an object-property puzzle: the shape of each object decides its new colour. Size does not work as a key (in pair 1 the size-12 and size-8 objects both become 1, while in pair 4 the size-10 object also becomes 1), but the number of enclosed holes does. My inspect counted, for each object, the background components fully inside the padded object crop, and printed the output colour at one of its cells:

| holes | output colour | examples |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1 | all the small single rings (sizes 8, 10, 12) |
| 2 | 3 | the stacked double rings (size 17, 16, 13) |
| 3 | 2 | the triple chains (size 18, 20, 25) |
| 4 | 4 | the long four-hole bar in pair 3 |

The table is consistent across all 15 objects in the four train pairs. The mapping is arbitrary (2 holes → 3, 3 holes → 2 is not a formula), so it is written as a lookup table, exactly as ARC legends usually are.

## Applying it to the test input

The test grid (15x17) has four 8-objects with 4, 3, 1 and 2 holes respectively, so they become colours 4, 2, 1 and 3. All four values appear in the train table, so nothing needs extrapolating. Positions are irrelevant: each object is recoloured in place.

## Construction stages

The program takes the objects in reading order, counts holes for each, and recolours the whole object as one edit, emitting a canvas after each object so the student sees one object change colour at a time; the last emit is the finished grid.
